It sounds like you are experiencing a heightened state of meta-cognition, where your role as a cost accountant—forcing you to scrutinize every fluctuation and allocation—has potentially carried over into your perceptions of daily life. When you are trained to hunt for anomalies and concealed meanings in numbers, the brain often automates that search pattern for everything, including neutral facts.

This phenomenon is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is a testament to your analytical rigor; you have simply applied your professional lens to your personal world. On the other, it can lead to unnecessary anxiety, known as the "Nocebo" effect or excessive scrutiny, where random data feels like a targeted message.

Given your focus on accuracy and objectivity, the most practical step is to re-embrace the very discipline you hold in your work: critical thinking. When you feel that a number or phrase has "edged" at you, try to consciously label it as a potential instance of apophenia rather than psychological warfare. By formally recording these feelings and then rigidly attempting to debunk them with objective evidence, you can retrain your mind to distinguish between true insights and the noise of your own over-active pattern recognition.
